land.text: the Norman realm of Roger II: Sicily, Malta, Calabria, Apulia and the duchy lands, without the Principality of Capua (Caserta block) and the Duchy of Naples

predecessors.note: The Hauteville realm of Roger II becomes a kingdom on 25 December 1130; Capua (1139) and Naples (1139) are added by conquest, see the ledger.

land.text: the island of Sicily and Malta, as Cliopatria's 1375 shape

successors.note: The Kingdom page infobox gives 'Sovereign state (1130-1410, 1713-1720, 1735-1816)' and says the island was 'added permanently to the Crown of Aragon as a result of the Compromise of Caspe of 1412'. Cliopatria's Crown of Aragon row already draws the island in 1290-1304 and from 1385; the eu-12 dossier should settle the overlap with this one.

capitals.name: Palermo
capitals.note: Infobox 'Capital and largest city: Palermo' (undated); Roger II crowned there in 1130 (E), Peter III 'marching to Palermo to be crowned' in 1282, Frederick III crowned there in 1296, Maria in 1377. The pages opened do not say where the Angevin kings (1266-1282) held court, nor name the mainland capital after 1282, which is the Kingdom of Naples' (Naples).

correction.text: the Norman realm of Roger II: Sicily, Malta, Calabria, Apulia and the duchy lands, without the Principality of Capua (Caserta block) and the Duchy of Naples

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1130-1136: Cliopatria's Kingdom of Sicily row starts in 1139, but 'The Norman Kingdom was sanctioned on Christmas Day, 1130, by Roger II of Sicily' who 'united the lands he had inherited from his father, Roger I of Sicily', including 'the Maltese Archipelago'. The land is Cliopatria's Norman Italy 1126 shape (79,542 km2; the 1139 shape is 80,288 km2) without the Caserta block: the Principality of Capua still stood (Robert 'expelled from Capua by July 1134', royal army invading it in 1138) and Naples was independent until 1139. No page gives an infobox area. [Reviewer eu-13-h, 2026-10-25: span extended from 1130-1136 to 1130-1138 and the kingdom-of-sicily_1137 keyframe removed, since Naples was absorbed in 1139, not 1137 (Norman conquest page: 'it was two years between Sergius' death and Naples' incorporation by Sicily').]

80,288 km2 for 1139-1146: the core plus Capua (Caserta block, 10 of 10 cells), Naples (2 cells) and Amalfi (1 cell). Roger II's page: after the capture of Pope Innocent II at Galluccio on 22 July 1139, 'by the Treaty of Mignano, the pope proclaimed Roger II rex Siciliae ducatus Apuliae et principatus Capuae' (the Kingdom page dates the treaty 25 March 1139, while 'three days later' from 22 July would be 25 July). The shape is right for 1139-1143; from 1144 the Abruzzi are added (see kingdom-of-sicily_1144).

correction.text: the mainland kingdom with the Abruzzi, after the October 1144 truce with the pope

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1144-1145: the northern frontier. Roger II's page: the mainland boundaries 'were only later fixed by a truce with the pope in October 1144', and Alfonso and Roger 'went off to conquer the Abruzzi'. Cliopatria adds 43 cells (L'Aquila, Teramo, Pescara, Chieti, Rieti edge; about 10,900 km2) only in 1147; the shape of 1147 is taken back to October 1144, a reading of the page's 'fixed'.

union.text: Tripoli (1146), Cape Bona (1148) and the Ifriqiya littoral

correction.text: the kingdom with its African possessions: Tripoli and the Ifriqiya littoral

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1146-1154: the African coast. 'Tripoli was captured in 1146 and Cape Bona in 1148'; Roger is 'King of Africa in 1148'; the Kingdom page says George of Antioch conquered the Ifriqiya littoral. Cliopatria has no African shape; the extent (the Tunisian east coast from Cape Bon to Sfax, and Tripoli) is a reading of 'the Ifriqiya littoral', not a surveyed line. The mainland and island are the 1147 shape.

correction.text: the kingdom with Mahdia as its last African stronghold

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1155-1159: 'In the mid-1150s, William lost the majority of his African possessions to a series of revolts'; 'in 1160, the final Norman African stronghold of Mahdia was taken by the Almohads'. Only Mahdia is kept in Africa for 1155-1159.

correction.text: unchanged shape, valid 1160-1201 (and the base of the African keyframes 1146-1159)

keyframe_review.note: 91,977 km2 for 1147-1201: Sicily, Malta and the mainland to the Abruzzi. The shape is right for 1160-1201 after the loss of Mahdia in 1160; for 1146-1159 the African overlay applies (see kingdom-of-sicily_1146 and _1155). The Kingdom page gives no area; 'the kingdom fell in 1194 to the House of Hohenstaufen' without a border change.

91,785 km2 for 1202-1259, two cells fewer than 1147 with no event on the pages opened: Henry VI and Constance crowned in 1194, Frederick II king from 1198 'a child who would also become Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II in 1220'. Cliopatria's personal union with the Empire (1216-1259) is not territory.

91,619 km2 for 1260-1271, one cell fewer; the Hohenstaufen fall comes with 'In 1266, conflict between the Hohenstaufen house and the Papacy led to Sicily's conquest by' Charles of Anjou, who 'defeated Manfred at the Battle of Benevento in 1266 and in 1268 Conradin at the Battle of Tagliacozzo'. No border change.

91,833 km2 for 1272-1278, the unified kingdom under Charles of Anjou. The Vespers page: 'in 1271 he seized control of Corfu and costal Albania' (Cliopatria draws the Angevin Greek and Albanian holdings in the separate House of Anjou-Sicily row from 1272).

correction.text: the unified kingdom of the Angevins, with its Greek scrap, until the Sicilian Vespers

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1279-1284 row is a 548 km2 scrap in Greece (22.9-23.1 E, 36.2-36.4 N) and the unified kingdom has vanished: the mainland has no shape at all until the Kingdom of Naples row of 1285, and the island none until 1305. The kingdom was whole until the revolt of 30 March 1282 ('Rebels took control over most of the island'), so 1279-1281 is the 1272 shape plus the Greek scrap; from 1282 see kingdom-of-sicily_1282.

correction.text: the island of Sicily and Malta under Peter III of Aragon and his sons

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1282-1304: the island kingdom. 'a revolt in 1282 known as the Sicilian Vespers threw off Angevin rule in the island of Sicily'; in early October 1282 'the remaining Angevin forces abandoned the island'; 'Though Sicily was lost, Charles' forces still controlled significant territories on mainland Italy'; the Peace of Caltabellotta made 'Sicily an independent kingdom' and the mainland 'the Kingdom of Naples'. Malta stayed Angevin until the relief fleet was beaten in 1283. Cliopatria shows nothing for the island in 1285-1289 and the Crown of Aragon row (76 Sicilian cells) in 1290-1304; this dossier holds that the island kingdom (Trinacria) is the Kingdom of Sicily throughout, under the House of Barcelona. The mainland, 1282-1284, has no Cliopatria shape.

22,876 km2 for 1305-1374: the island and Malta. 'In August 1302 the Treaty of Caltabellotta was signed, by which Frederick was recognised king of Trinacria'; 'the name Sicily was not to be used'. Reggio, taken in 1313, is a contest (ledger), not drawn here; the pages do not say it was held.

22,876 km2 for 1375-1384, the same island. From 1377 'the Kingdom of Sicily was ruled by four Vicars' who 'ruled effectively in their separate baronial lands alone' (no border change); Maria was seized in 1379 by Guglielmo Raimondo III of Moncada, 'Marquis of Malta and Gozzo'.

correction.text: the island of Sicily and Malta under Maria and Martin

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1385-1409: Cliopatria's row ends 1384 and its Crown of Aragon row takes the island from 1385, but Maria reigned 27 July 1377 to 25 May 1401 and 'In 1392 Maria and Martin returned with a military force and defeated the opposing barons, ruling jointly until Maria's death in 1401'; the Kingdom page's infobox has the sovereign state to 1410. The island stays this state's until 1410.

region.text: the Norman realm of Roger II: Sicily, Malta, Calabria, Apulia and the duchy lands, without the Principality of Capua (Caserta block) and the Duchy of Naples

ledger.note: 1130: Roger II is crowned king at Palermo. 'The Norman Kingdom was sanctioned on Christmas Day, 1130, by Roger II of Sicily'; 'Roger II united the lands he had inherited from his father, Roger I of Sicily'. Roger II's page: 'He was crowned in Palermo on Christmas Day 1130'.
1131: Amalfi submits. 'It was finally subdued in 1131 when Admiral John marched on it by land.' Roger II's page: 'In 1130, the Duchy of Amalfi revolted.'
1138: the royal army invades the Principality of Capua. 'in 1138 the royal army invaded the Principality of Capua'; Robert 'was expelled from Capua by July 1134' (the page's earlier phase).

1139: Naples joins the kingdom. 'On 30 October 1137, the last Duke of Naples died in the king's service at the Battle of Rignano', but 'it was two years between Sergius' death and Naples' incorporation by Sicily', and the page's 1139 paragraph has 'That year, Roger absorbed Naples into his kingdom'. Roger II's page has Sergius 'forced to acknowledge him as overlord of Naples' (1131). Cliopatria's Duchy of Naples row runs to 1138. [Reviewer eu-13-h, 2026-10-25: year corrected from October 1137 to 1139 on the Norman conquest page; the duchy-of-naples dossier also ends in 1139.]

1139: the pope recognises Roger. After Innocent II's capture at Galluccio on 22 July 1139, 'by the Treaty of Mignano, the pope proclaimed Roger II rex Siciliae ducatus Apuliae et principatus Capuae.' The Kingdom page dates the treaty 25 March 1139; Roger II's page implies 25 July.
1139: Capua is Roger's. 'rex Siciliae ducatus Apuliae et principatus Capuae', as proclaimed by the pope at the Treaty of Mignano. Cliopatria's Principality of Capua row ends in 1065.

region.text: the Abruzzi, the kingdom's northern march up to the frontier fixed by the truce

ledger.note: 1144: the northern frontier is fixed. The mainland boundaries 'were only later fixed by a truce with the pope in October 1144'; Alfonso and Roger 'went off to conquer the Abruzzi', with no result stated. The land is Cliopatria's 1147 addition, 43 cells in the Abruzzi.

ledger.counterpart: Tripoli (ruler not named on the page)
ledger.note: 1146: Tripoli. 'Tripoli was captured in 1146'; 'a series of conquests were made on the African coast' from 1146 to 1153.

1148: Cape Bon, and Roger 'King of Africa'. 'Tripoli was captured in 1146 and Cape Bona in 1148'; Roger is 'King of Africa in 1148'. The Kingdom page says George of Antioch conquered the Ifriqiya littoral, undated.

1148: the Ifriqiya littoral. The page's 'King of Africa in 1148' and 'a series of conquests on the African coast' from 1146 to 1153; the Tunisian east coast to Sfax is the researcher's reading of 'the Ifriqiya littoral' (Kingdom page). Cliopatria's Zirid row runs to 1151.

region.text: the majority of the African possessions

ledger.counterpart: African revolts (the page names no rulers)
ledger.note: 1155: most of Africa is lost. 'In the mid-1150s, William lost the majority of his African possessions to a series of revolts'; the year is the researcher's rounding of 'mid-1150s'. Mahdia is kept.
1160: Mahdia falls. 'in 1160, the final Norman African stronghold of Mahdia was taken by the Almohads.'

1194: the Hohenstaufen take the kingdom. 'the kingdom fell in 1194 to the House of Hohenstaufen'; 'William III of Sicily, the young son of Tancred, was deposed, and Henry and Constance were crowned as king and queen.'

1266: Charles of Anjou conquers the kingdom. 'In 1266, conflict between the Hohenstaufen house and the Papacy led to Sicily's conquest by' Charles, who 'defeated Manfred at the Battle of Benevento in 1266 and in 1268 Conradin at the Battle of Tagliacozzo.'

region.text: the mainland kingdom that stayed with Charles of Anjou

ledger.note: 1282: the Sicilian Vespers split the kingdom. 'a revolt in 1282 known as the Sicilian Vespers threw off Angevin rule in the island of Sicily' (30 March 1282); 'Though Sicily was lost, Charles' forces still controlled significant territories on mainland Italy.' The island carries on as this state; the mainland, as the Kingdom of Naples (Cliopatria row from 1285), is what the Peace of Caltabellotta later calls 'the Southern Italian territories of the former kingdom'.

region.text: Messina, the last Angevin port on the island

ledger.note: 1282: Messina. 'in early October 1282 Aragonese forces lifted the Messina siege, and the remaining Angevin forces abandoned the island'; at the revolt in March only Messina 'staying Angevin'.

1283: Malta. In summer 1283 'an attempt by an Angevin fleet to relieve Malta was intercepted and defeated by Lauria'; the page does not say that Malta fell, but Cliopatria's island kingdom includes Malta from 1305. Page silent on the capture.
1283: the war reaches Calabria. 'The Aragonese pressed their advantage and by February 1283 he had taken most of the Calabrian coastline.' The pages do not say how much of it was held later.

1296: Frederick is crowned king at Palermo. Frederick 'was crowned king by the nobles at Palermo in 1296' (infobox 25 March 1296, reign from 11 December 1295); James had forfeited the crown of Sicily to the papacy in 1295 by the Treaty of Anagni (Vespers page).

1302: the Peace of Caltabellotta ends the war on 31 August. 'The war ended in 1302 in the Peace of Caltabellotta, by which Sicily became an independent kingdom'; 'the Southern Italian territories of the former kingdom became the' Kingdom of Naples. The pages do not say what happened to the Calabrian coast.

1302: the island is recognised as the Kingdom of Trinacria. 'In August 1302 the Treaty of Caltabellotta was signed, by which Frederick was recognised king of Trinacria'; 'the name Sicily was not to be used'; 'At Frederick's death, the kingdom was to revert to the Angevins.'
1313: Frederick breaks the peace and takes Reggio. He 'in violation of the pact of Caltabellotta made war on the Angevins again (1313) and captured Reggio.'
1317: truce. 'A truce was concluded in 1317.' The page does not say whether Reggio was kept.

1377: Maria succeeds. 'After her father's death in 1377, she ascended the Sicilian throne' (reign 27 July 1377 to 25 May 1401); from 1377 'the Kingdom of Sicily was ruled by four Vicars' in their own baronial lands.

region.text: the island of Sicily and Malta

ledger.note: 1410: the sovereign kingdom ends. The infobox gives 'Sovereign state (1130-1410, 1713-1720, 1735-1816)'; the island 'was then added permanently to the Crown of Aragon as a result of the Compromise of Caspe of 1412'. The pages opened give no event for 1410 itself.

wars.name: Roger II's consolidation of the kingdom
wars.outcome: Roger lost at Nocera on 25 July 1132 and at Rignano on 30 October 1137 ('the greatest defeat of Roger II's career') yet absorbed Naples (1137) and Capua (1139); Innocent II was captured at Galluccio on 22 July 1139 and recognised him at Mignano.
wars.note: Bari fell to Lothair in June 1137 (Roger II's page); Lothair gave 'Capua and Apulia from the Kingdom of Sicily to Roger's enemies' (Kingdom page).

wars.name: Sicilian conquests on the African coast

zones.text: the African coast from Tripoli to Cape Bon and Mahdia

wars.outcome: Tripoli taken 1146, Cape Bona 1148; most of the African possessions lost to revolts in the mid-1150s, Mahdia to the Almohads in 1160.
wars.note: The Kingdom page adds that George of Antioch conquered the Ifriqiya littoral.

wars.name: Hohenstaufen conquest of the Kingdom of Sicily
wars.outcome: 'the kingdom fell in 1194 to the House of Hohenstaufen': William III deposed, Henry and Constance crowned. No border change.

wars.name: Angevin conquest of the Kingdom of Sicily
wars.outcome: Charles of Anjou, offered the crown by the papacy, 'defeated Manfred at the Battle of Benevento in 1266 and in 1268 Conradin at the Battle of Tagliacozzo.' No border change.
wars.note: The page dates the papal offer of the crown to Charles from 1262 (Urban IV, after talks with Manfred broke down); the war years are those of the two battles.

wars.name: War of the Sicilian Vespers

zones.text: the Calabrian coastline taken by Lauria by February 1283

wars.outcome: The island, lost to Angevin rule in March-October 1282, became 'an independent kingdom' at the Peace of Caltabellotta on 31 August 1302; the mainland became the Kingdom of Naples.
wars.note: Charles I of Anjou died at Foggia in early 1285, Peter III on 2 November 1285; James forfeited the crown of Sicily to the papacy at Anagni in 1295 (Vespers page).

wars.name: Wars between Frederick III and Robert of Naples
wars.outcome: Reggio captured in 1313; a truce in 1317; an Angevin fleet and army 'defeated at Palermo by Giovanni da Chiaramonte in 1325'. No lasting border change on the pages opened.
wars.note: The page does not date the end of the war beyond Frederick's death in 1337.

wars.name: Return of Maria and Martin
wars.outcome: 'In 1392 Maria and Martin returned with a military force and defeated the opposing barons'; the four vicars' baronial lands came back under the crown. No border change.
wars.note: Maria was kidnapped in 1379 by Moncada, 'Marquis of Malta and Gozzo', and handed to Peter IV's envoys in 1381.

certainty.note: The mainland frontiers moved with the war against Capua, Naples and the pope until the Treaty of Mignano.
The October 1144 truce with the pope fixed 'the mainland boundaries'; the rest are sea coasts. The African possessions of 1146-1160 are soft.
An island kingdom with sea coasts; the Calabrian ground of 1283-1302 and Reggio in 1313-1317 are contested and soft.

notes: The Kingdom of Sicily is treated as one state from 25 December 1130: the unified kingdom to the Vespers of 1282, then the island kingdom (Trinacria, under the House of Barcelona) to 1410, when the Kingdom page's infobox ends its sovereignty; the mainland that stayed with Charles of Anjou is the Kingdom of Naples (Cliopatria row from 1285, eu-13). The Peace of Caltabellotta (1302) is the treaty that 'divided the old Kingdom of Sicily in two'; this dossier splits the land in 1282 because the revolt was the de facto break. Cliopatria rows to correct elsewhere: (1) the Kingdom of Sicily row has no shape for 1285-1304 and a 548 km2 scrap in Greece for 1279-1284, so the Angevin mainland 1282-1284 and the island 1285-1304 are blank, apart from the Crown of Aragon row's island cells in 1290-1304; the Kingdom of Naples dossier should start in 1282 (or the colour agent should carry the mainland colour over). (2) The Crown of Aragon row (eu-12) draws the island in 1385-1409, which this dossier keeps as the Kingdom of Sicily's; one of the two should give way, or the Crown of Aragon should be drawn as a personal union. (3) House of Anjou-Sicily and Capetian House of Anjou (eu-10) share Wikidata Q939200; House of Anjou-Sicily's 1279-1284 row is the Angevin Albania, Corfu, Achaea and Malta (the Malta cell is in 1279 only), not the kingdom. (4) The Duchy of Naples row runs to 1138, a year after the pages' absorption; the Principality of Capua row ends in 1065 though the principality lasted to 1139. Pages disagree: the Kingdom page dates the Treaty of Mignano 25 March 1139, Roger II's page implies 25 July; the Kingdom page dates the end of sovereignty to 1410, Cliopatria's row ends 1384, and the Compromise of Caspe of 1412 made the union permanent. The Kingdom page also lists the state as sovereign in 1713-1720 and 1735-1816, beyond this dossier; the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and the Spanish and Austrian rule of the south are for other dossiers. Not on the pages opened: the Hohenstaufen succession by Manfred (1258), the Angevin court at Naples, the Treaty of Villeneuve 1372 (the Kingdom page: 'The division in the kingdom became permanent in 1372'), the Calabrian holdings after 1302 and the date of Reggio's recapture, the extent of the African possessions, and any infobox area (the Kingdom page gives none), so the area comparison could not be made; Cliopatria's 91,977 km2 for 1147-1201 is unchecked. No ruler strip is given because no page opened lists the kings in order. Vassalage: Cliopatria records a personal union with the Holy Roman Empire for 1216-1259; the Kingdom page gives Frederick II as emperor from 1220, and no event is drawn.
